## Synopsis: Definition of Microsurgery

- Microsurgery and supermicrosurgery refer to the surgical coaptation of small vessels.
- Usually around 1 mm in diameter or smaller.
- Performed under microscope magnification.
- Broad term: includes coaptation of tiny nerves and lymphatics, not just blood vessels.

## Synopsis: Evolution of the Technique

- Evolved significantly over the last four decades.
- Started with revascularization and replantation in 1960.
- Progressed to free flap surgery.
- Development of the operating microscope, microinstruments, and ultra-fine sutures aided widespread use.

## Synopsis: Common Techniques

- Most commonly used techniques:
  - End-to-end anastomosis
  - End-to-side anastomosis
  - Coupling devices
- Difficult situations (vessel discrepancy, inadequate length, poor quality) can be overcome with special techniques.

## Synopsis: High Success Rates

- Advances lead to consistently high success rates.
- Free tissue transfer is now a cost-effective, first-line option.
- Superior results and high patient satisfaction compared to conventional methods.
- Mentally and physically demanding; requires special training.

## Synopsis: Keys to Successful Free Flap Surgery

- Thorough preoperative planning.
- Flexibility of the surgical plan.
- Flawless execution.

## Synopsis: Monitoring and Pharmacological Agents

- Clinical assessment is the gold standard in free flap monitoring.
- Early detection of failing flap + prompt intervention = improved salvage rates.
- Useful pharmacological agents:
  - Low-dose heparin
  - PGE1
  - Dextran

## Synopsis: Avoiding Complications

- Complications are not only due to vascular compromise.
- Can be caused by:
  - Inadequate planning
  - Inappropriate flap selection
  - Flawed execution
- These can compromise the flap, functional, and aesthetic outcomes.

## Synopsis: Modern Success Rates

- Refined techniques and specialized microsurgical ICUs lead to 96–98% success rates in developed centers.
- If the first microsurgical reconstruction fails, a second attempt can yield good results after identifying and managing potential causes.

## Synopsis: Future of Microsurgery

- Microsurgery will continue to evolve.
- Has revolutionized reconstructive challenges.
- Wider application expected in:
  - Supermicrosurgery
  - Free-style free flaps
  - Composite tissue allotransplantation

## Introduction: General Terms

- **Microsurgery**: Surgery requiring an operating microscope or high magnification loupes.
- Sub-types based on structure:
  - Microvascular surgery (blood vessels ~1 mm)
  - Microneural surgery
  - Microlymphatic surgery
  - Microtubular surgery

## Introduction: Supramicrosurgery

- Extreme form of microsurgery.
- Anastomoses of vessels around 0.5 mm in diameter (0.3–0.8 mm).
- Common applications:
  - Lymphatic reconstruction
  - Perforator-to-perforator anastomosis/repair
  - Distal digital replantation

## Introduction: Reconstructive Microsurgery

- Utilizes microsurgical and supramicrosurgical techniques.
- Procedures include:
  - Revascularization
  - Replantation
  - Auto- or allotransplantation
- Solves problems from traumatic injuries, congenital deformities, and tumor ablation.
- Loupe magnification (×2.5–8) can be used for vessels/nerves around 2–3 mm.

## Introduction: Scope of Practice

- Microsurgical techniques are not limited to plastic surgery.
- However, plastic surgery has the most diverse scope of practice in modern surgery.

## Introduction: The Era of Microsurgery

- Began with the invention of the microscope in 1920.
- Leading factors for widespread use:
  - Improvement in magnification and illumination.
  - Development of microinstruments.
  - Development of ultrafine sutures.

## Introduction: Changing Indications

- Consistently high success rates (97–100%).
- Cost-effective with superior outcomes.
- Changed from being the "last resort" to the "first choice".
- Reversed and overthrew the reconstructive ladder in advanced centers.

## Introduction: Focus of the Chapter

- Principles and techniques of microsurgery, supermicrosurgery, and free tissue transfer.
- Includes perforator free flaps, free-style free flaps, allotransplantation, and future directions.
- Revascularization and replantation are covered in other chapters.

## Tools: Optical Systems

- Since Alexis Carrel's triangulation technique, anastomosed vessel diameters have become progressively smaller.
- Due to developments in:
  - Surgical techniques
  - Surgical instrumentation and microsutures
  - Improved optics in microscopes
- Magnification under adequate illumination allows accurate perception of anatomy.
- Reduces surgeon fatigue via improved ergonomics.

## Surgical Microscopes: Basic Features

- Binocular head with adjustable eyepieces.
- Teaching head for two people to work simultaneously.
- Potential third head for digital recording.
- Heads independently pivot with separate magnification levels.
- Can be retrofitted with a camera for real-time viewing and documentation.

## Surgical Microscopes: Controls

- Tilt, focus, and zoom controlled via:
  - Foot pedal (keeps hands free, requires coordination)
  - Hand control panel (practical, keeps functions in one place)
- Antimicrobial-coated surfaces and internally routed cables are important to prevent obstruction and bacterial harboring.

## Surgical Microscopes: Magnification Limits

- Up to 62× magnification provided by some microscopes.
- Instant magnification change for a variable working distance.
- Example: 10× eyepiece and 200 mm objective lens enables final magnification from 4.4 to 50.4 (Mitaka Kohki Co. Ltd.).

## Surgical Microscopes: Fluorescence Tools

- Microscopes like Leica and OPMI Pentero incorporate intraoperative fluorescence tools.
- Invaluable for:
  - Checking perfusion before and after surgery.
  - Lymphatic microsurgical reconstruction.
  - Precise tumor ablation in neurosurgery.

## Surgical Microscopes: Mounting Options

- Can be mounted on a stand.
- Placed on a table top.
- Worn on the surgeon's head.
- Hung on the ceiling or wall to conserve floor space.
- Movable microscopes are desired and cost-effective across specialties (ophthalmic ones may be an exception due to specialized needs).

## Surgical Microscopes: Magnification Levels

- Choosing the appropriate level of magnification is crucial.
- **Low magnification (6×–12×)**: Vessel preparation and suture tying.
- **Middle magnification (13×–15×)**: Suture placement.
- **High magnification**: Very small vessel anastomosis and inspection of the anastomosis.

## Box 25.1: Tips for Using Surgical Microscopes

- Familiarize yourself with the microscope.
- Spend time getting the position right (interpupillary distance and diopter correction).
- Use an adjustable seat if you intend to sit.
- Sit comfortably with feet flat on the ground for a stable base.
- Upper extremities should be well supported (resting on folded drapes) to minimize fatigue and tremor.
- Focus should be adjusted with the scope at highest magnification before starting.

## Loupes: Overview

- Provide magnifications of 2.5×–8×.
- Mounted on glasses or headbands.
- Advantages:
  - Cost-effective
  - Portable
  - Offer operator freedom
- Invaluable for precise dissection and placement of instruments/sutures.
- In experienced hands, can be an alternative to the microscope for vessels as small as 1 mm.

## Loupes: Loupes vs. Microscopes Study

- Retrospective study of 200 consecutive free microvascular tissue transplantations.
- Compared 3.5× loupes vs. operating microscope.
- Result: No difference in outcome. Free flap success rates of 99% for both groups.
- However, microscopes were required for:
  - Anastomoses in children.
  - Vessels of 1.5 mm or less in diameter.
- Most centers still use microscopes for greater magnification range and light sources.

## Loupes: Types - Compound (Galilean)

- Superior optics compared to single-lens reading glasses.
- Consist of two magnifying lenses separated by air.
- Achieve higher magnification, greater depth of field, and better working distance.
- Drawbacks:
  - Image quality distorts at magnifications above 2.5×.
  - Creates a "halo" effect at the periphery.
- Advantages: Relatively low cost and light weight.

## Loupes: Types - Prismatic

- Provide higher optical quality using a Schmidt prism.
- Lengthens the path of light through mirror reflections inside the loupe.
- Improved magnification, wider fields of view, longer depths of field/working distance.
- Drawbacks:
  - 30–40% heavier than compound loupes.
  - More expensive.
  - More easily damaged.

## Loupes: Choosing Magnification

- Dependent on surgeon's preference.
- **2.5×**: Often sufficient for hand surgery and flap harvesting.
- **3.5–4.5×**: Suitable for perforator dissection, thin flaps, or anastomoses.
- Note: Higher magnification decreases field of view and depth of field, while increasing weight.
- Loupes > 4.5× are cumbersome and cause neck tension/fatigue (microscope is better here).
- Experienced surgeons may perform standard perforator dissections without magnification.

## Loupes: Additional Features

- Once magnification is chosen, consider:
  - Lens design
  - Working angle and distances
- Mounting options:
  - Glasses or headbands
  - Through-the-lens (mounted to frames)
  - Flip-up or snap-fit type (allows cheaper changing of magnification/prescription)
- Manufacturers can supply headlights for additional lighting (useful with higher magnifications).

## Microsurgical Instruments: Overview

- Evolution of techniques required parallel refinements in instruments and suture materials.
- Many fine instruments originated from jewelers.
- A confusing array is available, but most microsurgery can be done with a surprisingly small set.

## Microsurgical Instruments: Essential Features

- Fine tips to spread, hold, or cut delicate tissue and suture.
- Nonreflective surface.
- Comfortable handles that close easily to prevent fatigue.
- Many are spring-loaded.
  - Too weak: tips close just by holding.
  - Too firm: hand fatigues quickly.

## Microsurgical Instruments: Material

- Most made of heat-hardened stainless steel (resistant to wear and tear).
- Prone to magnetization; store on demagnetized or nonmagnetic shelves.
- Demagnetizer: Placing instrument in a coil attached to AC supply and withdrawing slowly.
- Titanium is becoming popular:
  - Antimagnetic, rust-free, lighter weight.
  - In reality, can still become magnetized.

## Microsurgical Instruments: Handle Design

- Available with round or flat handles.
- Length: 10–18 cm depending on preference and working depth.
  - Shorter instruments: closer to surface (e.g., hand surgery).
  - Longer instruments (>18 cm): free tissue transfer.
- Longer instruments may be balanced with the balance point resting in the webspace.
- Slight counterweight at the end reduces fatigue and allows better control.

## Microsurgical Instruments: Maintenance

- Follow manufacturer instructions for maximal performance.
- Store in specially designed instrument cases.
- Protect fine tips with silicone or rubber tubes.
- Jaws must meet precisely.
- Use ONLY for handling vessels and nerves.
- Scrub nurse should regularly clean off blood/contaminants during surgery.
- Rinse with distilled or deionized water to avoid staining.
- Avoid high chloride concentrations (leads to pitting and corrosion).

## Types of Instruments: Scissors

- Spring-loaded with sharp, gently curved blades and slightly rounded tips.
- Can be used as a dissecting probe when held closed.
- Adventitia-trimming scissors: straight blades with sharp tips (also good for stitch-cutting).
- In reality, one curved scissor is adequate for both dissection and adventitia trimming.

## Types of Instruments: Needle Holders

- Spring-loaded, held like pencils, resting on the first web, supported by thenar muscles.
- Handle ideally rounded to allow rolling between fingers during needle passing.
- Jaws: thin, gently curved, narrow shoulders to grasp microsutures.
- Curved style is finer at the tip and more suitable for vessel dilatation.
- Ratchet lock available but not preferred (locking/unlocking damages needle and traumatizes tissue).
- Supermicrosurgery: Titanium preferred for lighter weight and custom manufacturing.

## Types of Instruments: Forceps

- Jeweler's forceps (originally by Swiss Dumont factory).
- Flat handle, sharply narrowing tips.
- Tips aligned with precision of 1/1000 inch (diameter of 10-0 nylon).
- Jaws should meet evenly over 3 mm length when closed with moderate pressure.
- Used continually in the nondominant hand for tissue handling, receiving needle, and tying.

## Types of Instruments: Forceps Variations

- Classified by width of contact surface, narrowness, and configuration.
- Wide jaws: can be used as needle holders.
- Straight/fine-pointed: suitable for tissue handling.
- Smooth-tipped (most common), toothed, curved, angled, or equipped with hole in tip.
- Angled forceps: useful for reaching under vessels, tying knots, patency tests.
- Modified slender, polished non-tapering tip: used to dilate vessels gently.
- Practical set: Titanium micro forceps (0.05 mm for 12-0, 0.1 mm for 10-0/11-0). Four micro forceps + one curved forceps are adequate.

## Types of Instruments: Vascular Clamps

- Evolved significantly from early bulldog clamps.
- Acland's double microvascular clamp (1974) largely superseded by Tamai's sliding bar modification.
- Ideally atraumatic with sufficient closing pressure to prevent bleeding/slippage without damaging vessel wall.
- Available as single or double approximator clamps.
- Divided into those for veins or arteries.

## Types of Instruments: Vascular Clamps (Cont'd)

- **Vein clamps**: Smaller closing pressure, flat jaw all the way to the end. Marked with "V".
- **Artery clamps**: Greater closing pressure, slight incurve at tip to prevent crushing. Marked with "A".
- Pressure is inversely proportional to vessel size.
- Ideal pressure: 5–10 g/mm² (largest vessels) to 15–20 g/mm² (smallest vessels in range).
- Use the smallest appropriate clamp to minimize crushing.

## Types of Instruments: Clampless Anastomosis

- Clamps can cause intimal lesions, occupy space, and risk backwalling.
- Atherosclerotic vessels are challenging.
- Clampless anastomosis uses a CE-certified thermosensitive gel.
  - Provides circular stenting and gentle distension.
  - Dissolves completely with cold saline irrigation.
- Other vascular surgery methods (LeGoo, aortic cannula with graft) have not been reported in microsurgery.

## Bipolar Coagulator

- Developed in 1956; promoted microsurgery by achieving a bloodless field.
- Conducts current between tips of jeweler's forceps.
- Produces heat damage only within a small area.
- Allows precise coagulation of branches as close as 2 mm to the main vessel.
- Power setting must be optimized to prevent spreading heat damage.
- Bipolar scissors are now commercially available.

## Irrigation and Suction

- Clear view of vessel walls is imperative.
- Irrigation purposes:
  - Prevent desiccation of vessels.
  - Prevent sticking of suture to tissue.
  - Wash away blood/clots.
  - Wash away prothrombotic factors.
- Performed with 5–10-mL syringe and lacrimal cannula/24-gauge angiocath.
- Suction methods: moistened hydrocellulose sponge, perforated background plate, homemade suction tips.
- Cellulose spearheads (eye sponges) afford precise control for small ooze.

## Microsutures: History

- Buncke described making the first microneedle by drilling a hole in a 75 mm stainless steel wire.
- Used to replant a rabbit's ear by anastomosis of 1 mm vessels.
- Acland developed the first commercially available needle with Springler–Tritt company.

## Microsutures: Sizes and Applications

- Available in combinations of materials, sizes (8-0 to 12-0), tensile strengths, and needle configurations.
- Standard means of vascular anastomosis.

| Suture | Needle Size | Vessel Diameter |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|
| 9-0 | 100 µm curved | 2 mm or more |
| 10-0 | 70–100 µm curved | 1 to 2 mm |
| 11-0 | 50–75 µm curved | Smaller vessels |
| 12-0 | 50 µm curved | Very small vessels |

## Microsutures: Needle Configurations

- Needle length preference: 5.1 mm for 9-0/10-0; 3.6 mm for 11-0/12-0.
- Shapes:
  - Three-eighths of a circle (typical)
  - Half-circle or straight (rarely used)
- Tip types:
  - Round
  - Tapered (commonly used)
  - Spatula-shaped (to prevent damage to vessel wall)
- Suture material: Non-resorbable nylon (low tissue reactivity, good knot-holding). Polypropylene preferred by some (slides/handles better).

## Anastomotic Devices: Overview

- Microsutures do not fully meet the criteria of an "ideal" anastomosis.
- Non-suture techniques developed for faster and less traumatic anastomosis.
- Ring–pin device (Nakayama 1962, Östrup/Berggren 1986) is the most successful and commonly used.
- Marketed as Microvascular Anastomotic COUPLER System (Synovis).

## Anastomotic Devices: Ring-Pin Coupler

- Consists of two disposable high-density polyethylene rings.
- Six to eight evenly spaced 0.16 mm diameter stainless-steel pins.
- Implanted with a reusable anastomotic instrument.
- Advantages:
  - Simple, fast, does not disturb the intima.
  - Patency rates up to 100%, even in irradiated fields.
- Sizes: 1 to 4 mm diameter (vessels 0.8–4.3 mm, max wall thickness 0.5 mm).
- Suitable for end-to-end and end-to-side anastomosis.

## Anastomotic Devices: Contraindications

- Contraindications for coupler:
  - Peripheral vascular disease
  - Areas with ongoing radiation therapy
  - Active infection
  - Concurrent diabetes
  - Corticosteroid therapy
- Contraindications for arterial use specifically:
  - Thick-walled vessels that do not adequately evert
  - Diameter discrepancies > 1.5:1 ratio
  - Non-pliable vessels (prior radiotherapy or calcification)
  - Any artery less than 1.5 mm in diameter

## Anastomotic Devices: Coupler Applications

- Experimental comparison (venous anastomosis):
  - Coupler: 100% patency
  - Sleeve technique: 80% patency
  - Standard end-to-end: 95% patency
- 1000 consecutive venous anastomoses in breast reconstruction (Jandali et al.):
  - Anastomotic time: 2–6 minutes.
  - Patency rate: 99.4%. No total flap losses.
- Effective in end-to-side anastomosis of veins in head/neck recon (99–100% patency).
- Absorbable coupler developed to resolve permanent rigid ring issue (95% clinical patency; absorbed at 70 days to 30 weeks).

## Anastomotic Devices: Other Couplers

- Vacuum-assisted microvascular anasto-coupler:
  - Uses negative pressure as an atraumatic force instead of pins.
  - Only tested on rats; no clinical applications to date.
- Nonpenetrating microvascular stapler (VCS clip applier system):
  - Uses nonpenetrating titanium clips in an interrupted, everting fashion.
  - Four sizes (0.9 to 3.0 mm).
  - Reduced anastomotic time, higher patency rate.
  - Requires stay sutures and everting forceps.

## Other Non-Suture Methods: Glues

- **Fibrin glues**:
  - Two components: fibrinogen/factor XIII/plasma proteins + thrombin/aprotinin/calcium chloride.
  - Imitates final coagulation pathway.
  - Reduces number of sutures required and anastomotic time.
  - Drawbacks: Potential luminal entry, allergic reactions, anaphylaxis.
- **Cyanoacrylates**:
  - Plagued by histotoxicity, foreign-body granulomatous response, vessel wall thinning, elastic lamina splitting, media calcification.
  - 2-Octyl-cyanoacrylate might be less toxic.

## Other Non-Suture Methods: Laser Welding

- Welding with thermal or laser energy long advocated.
- Types: Nd:YAG, CO2, argon, diode lasers.
- Show up to 100% patency rates and better blood flow in veins.
- Laser-activated protein solders introduced for more strength.
- Diode laser-assisted anastomosis shows equal survival, shorter time, faster healing.
- Limitation: Fear of weakening site and pseudoaneurysm formation.
- Clinical study: 96.6% success rate (1 rupture, 3 hematomas).

## Other Non-Suture Methods: Stents and Magnets

- Cylindrical or T-shaped intravascular stents (experimental).
- External metallic ring to keep cylindrical form and avoid through-stitching.
- Magnets:
  - First tested by Obora in 1978.
  - Tested on large animal models for side-to-side AV or vein graft anastomoses.
  - Deployment device inserts magnets, which attract and compress arterial wall forming a two-magnet vascular port.

## General Principles: Working Environment

- Prerequisites: Calm disposition and patience.
- Concentrate without unnecessary interruptions; do not be hurried.
- Justifiable to take breaks during long sessions.
- Competent assistant and specialized scrub nurse make a big difference.
- Microsurgeons often operate late, alone, or on challenging vessels.
- Endurance and perseverance are virtues.

## General Principles: Training

- "Some are born microsurgeons while others become so through discipline and training."
- Traditional apprenticeship is hard to apply; specialized fellowship is a must.
- Lab training progression:
  1. Familiarizing with instrument handling under magnification.
  2. Suturing stretched surgical gloves or silicone tubes.
  3. Live anastomoses in a rat model.
- Alternatively, trainees learn from senior surgeons clinically.

## General Principles: Clinical Training Progression

- Trainees usually do the second vein first.
- After achieving steady patency, the arterial anastomosis is handed to them under supervision.
- Must be able to do both vein and artery well multiple times before operating alone.
- Trainees encouraged to report honestly and call for help instead of wasting time.
- If there is deviation from acceptable standards, the experienced member should immediately take over.

## General Principles: Planning and Positioning

- Time spent planning and positioning is never wasted.
- Right position = easier movements and faster progress.
- Comfort relates directly to success.
- Two-team approach reduces operating time.
- Proper patient positioning alleviates need to reposition during surgery.

## General Principles: Surgeon Positioning

- If seated on a self-adjustable stool:
  - Legs under operating table, feet flat on ground (stable base).
  - Forearms rest on folded drapes at the same level as anastomosis.
- Minimizes tremor and fatigue.
- Microscope positioned to not obstruct movement while providing maximum control.
- Microscope base fixed to allow sufficient room for maneuvering.

## General Principles: Securing the Flap Inset

- Inset is considered *before* anastomosis is performed.
- After circulation is restored, flap swells and bleeds, making deep inset difficult (especially in head/neck).
- Partial/complete inset before anastomosis allows accurate judgment of pedicle length (avoids tension/redundancy).
- Tailoring/thinning is better performed while flap is perfused to control bleeders and avoid hematoma.
- Exception: Breast surgery (inset done after anastomosis if anastomosis lies deep to inset).

## General Principles: Recipient Vessel Selection

- Use healthy recipient vessels of appropriate size with good flow.
- Away from zones of trauma, irradiation, inflammation, fibrosis, and scarring.
- Healthy vessel: Soft wall, easily dissected vascular sheath.
- Traumatized vessel: Encased in fibrotic tissue, prone to bleeding.
- Perforating branches can be used instead of classic big vessels (extremity and breast recon).

## Recipient Vessels: Assessment

- Assessment needed following irradiation, stiff neck, osteoradionecrosis, multiple free flaps, single-vessel leg, trauma, DVT history, diabetes, atherosclerosis, advanced lymphatic disease.
- Doppler ultrasound for leg vessels.
- Angiography/CTA indicated when in doubt about availability/quality (e.g., non-palpable pedal pulses).
- Normal findings may not always translate into healthy usable vessels.
- Indocyanine green (ICG) imaging and lymphoscintigraphy for lymphatic surgery planning.

## Recipient Vessels: Preparation

- Done under loupes or microscope magnification.
- Dissect sufficient length for tension-free anastomosis.
- Deep vessels (e.g., internal thoracic) require greater length to orientate superficially.
- Gross trimming of adventitia performed around anastomosis area.
- Quality of artery and vein must be checked under microscope for signs of damage.

## Figure 25.1: Horizontal Vessel Orientation

- **Figure Description**: Horizontal vessel orientation allows both lumens of the vessel to be adequately visualized.
- This facilitates accurate suture placement and alignment during anastomosis.

## Recipient Vessels: Checking Arterial Flow

- Vital to check flow within the artery.
- Expansile pulsation indicates adequacy; confirm with healthy spurting from divided vessel.
- If no good spurt:
  - Check if patient is normotensive.
  - Take steps to relieve vasospasm.
  - Cut back vessel until healthy spurtting is encountered.
- Apply vascular clip while waiting for flap harvest/inset.

## Recipient Vessels: Vein Assessment

- Ideal recipient vein: At least as wide as the flap vein.
- Smaller diameter may cause bottle-neck effect and compromise drainage.
- Divide vein to assess quality; good outflow indicates healthy vessel.
- If in doubt, catheterize lumen and flush heparinized saline.
  - Little/no resistance = good drainage.
  - High pressure = tie off tributaries to reduce backflow.
- Apply single or double clamp for anastomosis.

## Recipient Vessels: Irrigation and Spasm Prevention

- Irrigate vessels with heparinized saline during and after dissection.
- Cover vessels with 2–4% lidocaine or 3% papaverine-soaked gauze.
- Prevents desiccation and vasospasm.
- When ready for revascularization, place vessel ends in double approximating clamp under microscope.
- Use moist gauze beneath vessel to elevate plane, orientate horizontally, and mop up pooling fluids.
- Silastic tube attached to suction can facilitate drainage without risking vessel suction.

## Preparation of Vessels: Inspection

- Inspect lumens for irregularities:
  - Intimal tears or separation from media
  - Thrombi
  - Atherosclerotic plaques
  - Friable calcified walls
- Gently irrigate debris away or remove atraumatically with microforceps.
- If unsuccessful, cut back vessel to attain healthier segment (without compromising pedicle length).
- Suboptimal intima occasionally accepted; outcome dependent on meticulous technique.

## Figure 25.2: Loose Intima

- **Figure Description**: Illustrates various vessel wall pathologies.
  - Friable walls
  - Separation of intimal walls
  - Separation of medial walls
  - Intraluminal valves, clots, flaps, tears
  - Branches near anastomosis
- These irregularities must be identified before anastomosis.

## Figure 25.3: Intraluminal Irrigation of Vessels

- **Figure Description**: Shows the process of gently irrigating the vessel lumen.
- Purpose is to clear blood, clots, and debris to provide a good view and wash away prothrombotic factors.
- Ensures a clean environment for suture placement.

## Preparation of Vessels: Wall Anatomy

- **Tunica Intima**: Innermost layer. Single layer of endothelium on basal lamina. Thin subendothelial layer. Separated by internal elastic lamina.
- **Tunica Media**: Mainly smooth-muscle cells. Thickest layer in arteries. Much thinner in veins (sometimes indistinguishable in lesser veins).
- **Tunica Adventitia**: Outermost layer. Loose areolar connective tissue containing vasa vasorum.

## Figure 25.4: Cross-Sectional View of Artery and Vein

- **Figure Description**: Compares the cross-sectional layers of an artery (left) and a vein (right).
- Shows the relative thickness of the tunica intima, internal elastic lamina, tunica media, and tunica adventitia.
- Veins have less defined layers, particularly the tunica media.

## Preparation of Vessels: Adventitia Trimming

- Loose adventitia peeled off using microforceps or sharply trimmed.
- Pull towards lumen and cut parallel to luminal edge (distance of 3–4 mm from anastomotic site).
- Neither method removes all adventitia; sharp dissection causes less damage.
- Purpose: Improve visualization, prevent adventitia from falling into lumen during knot tying.
- Radical trimming: Cut tented adventitia parallel to vessel length, avoid injuring tunica media.
- Overly aggressive stripping causes necrosis/false aneurysms.

## Figure 25.5: Sharp Trimming of Adventitia

- **Figure Description**: Demonstrates the technique of sharply trimming the adventitia.
- The adventitia is pulled towards the lumen and cut parallel to the luminal edge to prevent it from prolapsing into the vessel lumen.

## Figure 25.6: More Radical Resection of Adventitia

- **Figure Description**: Shows the meticulous cutting of tented adventitia parallel to the length of the vessel.
- Care is taken to avoid injuring the tunica media during this more radical resection.

## Preparation of Vessels: Dilation

- Gently dilate lumens in two different planes with vessel dilator or microneedle holder.
- Maintain stretch for one second.
- Benefits:
  - Aids suturing process.
  - Prevents vasospasm.
  - Allows intraluminal blood to be flushed out.
  - Overcomes minor size discrepancies.
- Blood beyond clamps in undamaged vessels is not at risk of clotting.

## Figure 25.7: Gentle Luminal Dilatation of the Vessel End

- **Figure Description**: Illustrates the gentle dilation of the vessel lumen in two different planes.
- The stretch is maintained for about one second to aid suturing and prevent vasospasm.

## Figure 25.8: Bringing Clamps Together

- **Figure Description**: Shows a hemostat artery forceps bringing the two clamps towards each other.
- The vessel ends are positioned to just touch or have minimal overlap for anastomosis.

## Anastomoses Sequence: General Rules

- No consensus regarding optimal sequence.
- Ischemia time and relative vessel position dictate order.
- Deeper, more difficult-to-reach vessel is usually repaired first.
- If anatomy doesn't restrict, arterial repair first may shorten warm ischemia time.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Artery First

- **Advantages**:
  - Shortens warm ischemia time.
  - Re-establishment of circulation reveals dominant venous drainage.
  - Helps detect twist, kink, or compression in pedicle.
- **Disadvantages**:
  - Flap may start bleeding, affecting vein anastomosis.
  - Venous congestion may increase bleeding and allow buildup of free radicals.
- Solution: Allow second comitant vein to drain freely into gauze away from the field.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Vein First

- Allows for better adjustment of pedicle length.
- Delays revascularization of the flap.
- Experimental studies show highest failure rate if artery is done first and immediately unclamped (due to venous congestion).
- Other studies show no optimal sequence.
- Authors' practice: Routinely repair artery first and leave unclamped during vein repair. Allow less dominant vein to drain freely.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Number of Venous Anastomoses

- Some advocate two venous anastomoses to avoid venous insufficiency.
  - Khouri et al.: 4.3% failure with one vs. 0% with two.
- Single venous anastomosis to a suitable recipient vein provides adequate drainage and reduces operative time.
  - Futran and Stack: Equivalency in survival with single vs. dual in radial forearm flaps.
- Sound judgment required: If first vein is less reliable/uncertain, perform a second.
- Flap anatomy and chimeric design could benefit from dual venous anastomoses.

## Suturing Techniques: End-to-End Anastomosis

- Most common method.
- Simple and appropriate for most arterial and venous anastomoses.
- Techniques:
  - Halving
  - Triangulation
  - "Back wall-up"
- Carrel's principles:
  - Avoid luminal narrowing.
  - Avoid creation of folds and rough inner surface.
  - Oppose two intimal edges closely.

## Figure 25.9: Interrupted Suturing Techniques

- **Figure Description**: Shows placement of three stay sutures at 120° or 180° to ease subsequent placement of sutures.
- Cobbett modified Carrel's 3-stay technique to 2 stays at 120°. Tensioning apart makes the back wall fall away, reducing through-stitch risk.
- Alternatively, 2 stay sutures at 180° ensures even spacing.

## End-to-End: Suture Placement

- Needle should penetrate vessel wall perpendicularly, incorporating all layers (especially intima).
- Bite size determined by wall thickness and suture; maintained throughout.
- First throw should be double to maintain intended tension.
- Two single throws follow to complete the knot.
- Knots snugged down by sight, stopping when edges meet and slightly evert.

## End-to-End: Knot Tying Precautions

- Sutures too tight:
  - Small tears expose subendothelium.
  - Platelet aggregation and thrombus formation.
  - Damage to media; if 1/3 of wall necroses, re-endothelialization fails and lumen occludes.
  - Narrowing of anastomosis site.
- Leave last few stitches untied until the last suture is placed, then tie in turn.
- Leave apparent gaps alone until clamp is released and vessel refills to prevent through stitching.

## Figure 25.10: Knot Tying with a Double Throw

- **Figure Description**: Demonstrates the technique of tying a knot with a double throw.
- The double throw ensures the intended tension is maintained during the anastomosis.

## End-to-End: Continuous Suturing

- Suitable for minimally size-discrepant vessels > 2 or 3 mm.
- Reduces anastomosis time by nearly half. More hemostatic.
- Problems: Suture entanglement, purse-string constriction.
- Technique: Place 2-3 stay sutures. Running sutures placed at regular intervals and tied to next stay suture. Turn double clamp over and continue.
- Patency rates of 97.5–100% achievable.

## Figure 25.11: Placing a Halving Suture

- **Figure Description**: (A) and (B) show how placing a halving suture may facilitate accurate stitch placement.
- This is performed when executing an end-to-end anastomosis using interrupted suturing.

## Figure 25.12: Back Wall First

- **Figure Description**: Illustrates the "back wall-up" technique.
- The first suture is placed posterocentrally. Subsequent sutures are placed on either side, working around the circumference.

## Figure 25.13: Continuous Suture Technique

- **Figure Description**:
  - (A) Complete anastomosis using one continuous suture.
  - (B) Using stay sutures placed at 180° and performing continuous sutures between the two and tying off to each stay suture prevents purse-stringing of the lumen.
- Meticulous attention prevents purse-string effect.

## End-to-End: Open-Loop Suturing

- Combines convenience of continuous running suture with advantages of interrupted suturing.
- Running suture performed leaving loops small enough that they do not flop.
- First suture tied and cut short. Next loop pulled through and tied, repeated until all loops tied.
- Reduces maneuvers and needle handling.
- Maximal lumen visualization maintained. Eliminates purse-stringing.
- Requires practice to avoid loop entanglement.

## Figure 25.14: Open-Loop Suture

- **Figure Description**: Visualizes the open-loop suturing technique.
- Loops are left untied initially and then sequentially pulled through and tied to complete the anastomosis.

## End-to-End: Sleeve Anastomosis

- Variant of end-to-end ("end-in-end") introduced by Lauritzen (1978).
- Telescopes vessels using two extraluminal sutures pulling one vessel inside the other.
- Fewer sutures = reduced time and trauma.
- Low patency rates prevented popularity.
- Modification: "Hemi-invagination" by Riggio et al. improved patency to 95–100% (side cut on overlapping vessel + stitch at apex). Only tested on rats.

## Figure 25.15: Sleeve Anastomosis

- **Figure Description**: Demonstrates the sleeve anastomosis technique.
- One vessel is telescoped inside the other using extraluminal sutures.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Indications

- Particularly useful for:
  - Significant vessel size discrepancy.
  - Significant wall thickness discrepancy.
  - Need to preserve distal circulation (e.g., single-vessel leg).
- Anecdotally less prone to vessel spasm in lower extremity.
- Higher success rates, but not necessarily higher patency rates compared to end-to-end.

## End-to-Side: Arteriotomy/Venotomy

- Create triangular, elliptical, or longitudinal slit opening.
- Opening opens up due to muscle contraction.
- No irregular edges (weakens wall, facilitates thrombus).
- Dissect sufficient length for two clamps. Trim adventitia circumferentially.
- Baby Satinsky clamp useful to maintain flow and is less traumatic.
- Vascular slings can be double-looped to act as stabilizers.

## Figure 25.16: Making the Arteriotomy

- **Figure Description**: Shows the end-to-side anastomosis process.
- A single transverse stitch is taken as a stay suture. Vessel is excised using microvascular scissors and extended with a No. 11 blade.
- Acland–Banis arteriotomy clamp can be used to hold and excise an ellipse.

## End-to-Side: Suturing Technique

- Opening should not be longer than donor vessel diameter (stretches when clamps released).
- If flap vessel is long enough: Stay stitches at distal/proximal ends. Front wall completed, then pull vessel towards you for back wall (Godina).
- If insufficient length: Wall further from you must be performed first.
- Sutures placed radially to the center of the arteriotomy.
- Transversely placed sutures may cause severe leakage at distal/proximal ends.

## Figure 25.17: Back Wall First

- **Figure Description**: Shows end-to-side anastomosis in cases where there is insufficient length to rotate the vessel.
- The back wall needs to be sutured first to ensure proper closure and patency.

## End-to-Side: Godina's Advantages

- According to Godina, advantages included:
  - Higher success rate.
  - Greater freedom of operative planning.
  - Technical simplicity in terms of access to vessels.
- However, studies show end-to-end and end-to-side are equally effective when properly applied (patency approaches 100%).
- End-to-side venous anastomosis had higher success rate than end-to-end in one rat study.
- Slit technique easier than hole technique for vessels < 1.5 mm.

## Use of the Coupler: Technique

- Most common alternative to conventional suture.
- Time-saving with equivalent patency rates.
- Measure outer diameter of each vessel after gentle dilatation.
- For size-discrepant vessels: Coupler internal diameter = outer diameter of smaller vessel.
- Load device onto anastomotic instrument. Place perpendicular to vessels.
- Thread vessel end through ring. Impale edges securely on pins (1-2 pin diameters with adequate intimal bite).
- Impale every other pin first, then intermediate pins. Draping flap vessel first is easier.
- Bring rings together (clockwise), reinforce with hemostat. Eject device (counterclockwise).

## Figure 25.18: Application of the Coupler Device

- **Figure Description**:
  - (A) The vessel is oriented at 90° to the applicator and the vessel end impaled evenly on the pins.
  - (B) The vessel is anastomosed and released by turning the applicator handle.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Size-Discrepant Vessels

- Commonly encountered.
- Bigger problems if inflow recipient is big & flap artery is small, OR outflow flap is big & recipient vein is small.
- Sudden caliber change causes turbulence predisposing to thrombosis.
- Mismatches up to 4:1 can be anastomosed end-to-end depending on skill.

## Figure 25.19: Size-Discrepant Vessels

- **Figure Description**:
  - (A) The smaller vessel end can be dilated and stretched to match the larger one, cut obliquely to increase the diameter, or a longitudinal side cut of the smaller vessel can be made. (Angles > 30° may cause kinking).
  - (B) The smaller vessel is sutured as widely as possible to the larger vessel. A clip is brought across obliquely to taper the remaining end of the larger vessel, reducing turbulence.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Managing Discrepancy

- Simplest method: Gently stretch smaller vessel mechanically.
- Place interrupted sutures further apart on the larger vessel.
- Fish-mouth incision or oblique cut on smaller vessel.
- Perform anastomosis distal to a side branch; open distal wall so V shape is the vessel end.
- Discrepancy > 3:1: Consider end-to-side, vein graft, or side branch of larger vessel.
- Last resort: Dilate smaller vessel maximally, suture widely to larger vessel, suture remaining vessel to itself, obliquely place surgical clip to taper.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Wall Thickness Discrepancy

- Does not usually pose a problem.
- Gentle dilatation thins the wall.
- For persistent discrepancy:
  - Take equal bites of intima from both vessels.
  - Incorporate less of media and adventitia of the thicker-walled vessel.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Vertically Oriented Anastomosis

- Most challenging configuration.
- Strategies:
  - Change position of body part, table, or yourself to make it horizontal.
  - Free up more vessel length to manipulate into horizontal plane with gauze.
  - Reduce magnification (increases depth of field, reduces need to alter focus constantly).

## Difficult Anastomosis: Atherosclerosis

- Common in elderly, cardiovascular disease, and irradiation-induced atherosclerosis.
- If significant plaque found: Cut back to healthier intima or choose another vessel.
- Divide artery with sharp scissors in one cut to minimize intimal separation.
- Trimming: Slowly and circumferentially, resembling opening a can (not guillotine).

## Difficult Anastomosis: Atherosclerosis (Cont'd)

- Clamp tension: Do not exert too much to avoid fracturing calcified walls. Use venous microclamps for less pressure.
- Sutures: Use round needle, smallest microsuture, meticulous interrupted placement.
- Pass suture from inside lumen to outside to avoid further intimal separation.
- If both vessels diseased: Use double-needle suture, or careful counterpressure with forceps within vessel.
- Avoid vessel dilatation.
- End-to-end preferred over end-to-side (less exposure of plaque edges).

## Figure 25.20: Counterpressure for Intima

- **Figure Description**: Shows the use of forceps to provide counterpressure to minimize trauma and separation of the intima.
- This is crucial when suturing atherosclerotic vessels to prevent creating intraluminal flaps.

## Microvascular Grafts: Overview

- Increased flap options and proper planning have diminished the need for vein grafts.
- Still necessary in trauma, vessel-depleted neck, and re-explorations.
- Association with complication/failure may reflect case complexity, vessel quality, and hematoma rather than the graft itself.
- Other studies show patency and survival are not reduced by vein grafts.

## Microvascular Grafts: Indications

- Recipient vessel out of reach of pedicle or under tension.
- Considerable size mismatch.
- Need to place anastomosis outside zone of injury/radiation.
- Y-shaped vein graft can restore circulation to distal stump.

## Microvascular Grafts: Harvest Principles

- Harvest is just as important as anastomosis; done with loupe magnification.
- Match caliber of graft to vessels.
- Upper limb defects bridged with upper limb veins.
- Workhorse: Great/lesser saphenous vein (length, two-team approach).
- Alternatives: Cephalic, comitant veins, volar forearm, dorsal foot veins.
- All grafts need dilatation prior to anastomosis.
- Narrow venous flap can solve arterial gap + lack of soft-tissue cover simultaneously.

## Microvascular Grafts: Vein Grafts

- Handle vein minimally; ligate/coagulate tributaries.
- Mark length required (grafts contract after division, lengthen with high-pressure flow -> risk of kinking).
- Direction is crucial due to valves; must have antegrade flow.
- Mark proximal end with surgical clip.
- Hydrodilatation stretches graft, untwists vein, relieves spasm, visualizes bleeding points.
- Anastomose open end first, release clamp to check direction and redundancy.

## Microvascular Grafts: Arterial Grafts

- Advantages over vein grafts:
  - Absence of valves.
  - Anatomical taper.
  - Similar luminal and wall-thickness profiles.
  - Better handling characteristics.
  - Maintain endothelium; less subintimal hyperplasia.
  - More prostacyclin in first 3 weeks (greater antithrombogenic activity).
- No significant proven advantages in microvascular surgery context.
- Harvest sites: Subscapular tree, anterior/posterior interosseous arteries, radial/ulnar arteries, deep/superficial inferior epigastric artery, dorsalis pedis artery.

## Testing Patency: Observation

- Assess after completion of each anastomosis and periodically through operation.
- **Arterial pulsation**:
  - Expansile: Normal.
  - Longitudinal (long axis): Sign of partial/complete thrombosis. No return of circulation. Redo anastomosis.
- **Vein patency**: Good flow, natural round diameter.
  - Engorged, dark blood column = thrombosed. Reanastomose.
  - Engorgement of secondary veins, continuous dark bleeding from flap edges = non-patent venous anastomosis.

## Testing Patency: Physical Tests

- **Uplift test**: Gently hook up thin-walled vessel until blood column almost occluded. Alternate filling and collapsing with each pulse indicates patency.
- **Empty-and-refill test**: Gently occlude vessel distal to anastomosis. With second forceps, empty a segment next to first pair, running in direction of flow. Release first pair. Immediate refill = patent. Sluggish/absent = not patent.
  - Slightly traumatic; perform only when needed, preferably on veins.

## Figure 25.21: Empty-and-Refill Test

- **Figure Description**: Illustrates the empty-and-refill (patency) test.
- Two pairs of forceps are used distal to the anastomosis to empty a vessel segment. Releasing the proximal forceps allows immediate refill if the anastomosis is patent.

## Testing Patency: Alternative Methods

- **Side branches**: Atraumatic way to assess arterial flow and venous outflow. Requires awareness during dissection to keep side branches.
- **Indocyanine Green (ICG)**: Easier and more accurate.
  - Microscopes equipped with infrared cameras.
  - Handheld devices available to examine flap perfusion.

## General Aspects of Free Flap Surgery

- First clinical application of microsurgery was replantation, which evolved into free flap surgery.
- Requires thorough preoperative planning, flexibility, and flawless execution.
- Success is multifactorial, heavily dependent on technical anastomosis skills.
- High success rates (96–98%) make it a first-line, cost-effective option in modern reconstructive surgery.

## Conclusion: The Evolution Continues

- Microsurgery has reversed the reconstructive ladder.
- Demands experience, resources, specialized infrastructure, and training.
- Future applications expanding into:
  - Supermicrosurgery
  - Free-style free flaps
  - Composite tissue allotransplantation
- The field continues to evolve with technological and pharmacological innovations.

## Summary: Key Takeaways

- Microsurgery involves coaptation of tiny vessels, nerves, and lymphatics under magnification.
- Essential tools: Surgical microscopes, loupes, microinstruments, microsutures, and anastomotic devices.
- Techniques: End-to-end, end-to-side, continuous, open-loop, and sleeve anastomosis.
- Difficult situations (size discrepancy, atherosclerosis, vertical orientation) require specialized maneuvers.
- Vein or arterial grafts may be necessary despite advanced planning.
- Patency testing and clinical assessment are critical for flap survival.
- High success rates solidify microsurgery as a premier reconstructive option.
